articles.title: 8 Dead, 25 Injured as Truck Rams into Ganesh Immersion Procession in Hassan
articles.author: The Times Patriot
articles.excerpt: Hassan (Karnataka): A Ganesh idol immersion procession turned tragic in Mosale Hosahalli village, Hassan district, when a truck lost control and rammed into devotees on Friday night.

body.html:
Hassan (Karnataka):
A Ganesh idol immersion procession turned tragic in Mosale Hosahalli village, Hassan district, when a truck lost control and rammed into devotees on Friday night.

🔴 Casualties:
● At least 8 people killed (5 on the spot, 3 at hospitals)
● 25 others injured, 18 admitted to Hassan Institute of Medical Sciences (HIMS), others in private hospitals

🔴 Cause:
Police said the truck, traveling on NH-373, lost control while trying to avoid a motorbike. The driver, who was also injured, has been taken into custody.

🔴 Reactions:
● CM Siddaramaiah and Deputy CM DK Shivakumar expressed deep grief and announced ₹5 lakh compensation for each victim’s family.
● The state government will bear medical expenses of the injured.
● Union Minister HD Kumaraswamy also called the mishap “horrific” and urged free treatment.

Villagers reported chaotic scenes as the truck ploughed into the crowd amid DJ music during the immersion. Shocking visuals of the accident have surfaced.

#HassanAccident #Karnataka #GaneshImmersion #BreakingNews #RoadAccident #Hassan #NH373

articles.title: Supreme Court Issues Four-Step Test to Quash False Rape Cases
articles.author: The Times Patriot
articles.excerpt: The Supreme Court has recently delivered a significant judgment, directing High Courts to adopt a clear four-step test before quashing criminal proceedings in cases involving allegations of rape on the false promise of marriage.

body.html:
The Supreme Court has recently delivered a significant judgment, directing High Courts to adopt a clear four-step test before quashing criminal proceedings in cases involving allegations of rape on the false promise of marriage.

A bench of Justice JB Pardiwala and Justice Sandeep Mehta observed that if a case is based purely on false or frivolous allegations, allowing it to continue would amount to gross misuse of the legal process.

The court clarified that whenever a petition is filed under Section 482 of the CrPC (now Section 528 of the Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita) seeking to quash such cases, High Courts must carefully examine four aspects:

1. Are the materials presented by the accused solid, undisputed, and unimpeachable?
2. Do these materials fully disprove the complaint to the extent that any reasonable person would dismiss the allegations outright?
3. Are these materials such that the complainant or prosecution has not, or cannot, reasonably dispute them?
4. Would continuing the trial defeat the ends of justice and amount to abuse of court process?

If the answer to all four is “yes,” the High Court should not hesitate to dismiss such cases immediately.

The bench emphasized that dragging a person into a criminal trial on false allegations is no trivial matter. Such accusations damage reputations and waste valuable judicial time. The court also stressed that in cases of rape allegations on the basis of a false marriage promise, courts must carefully assess whether the accused genuinely intended to marry or merely lured the complainant into a physical relationship with a false assurance.

This ruling came in the case of Pradeep Kumar Kesari vs. State of Uttar Pradesh. In August 2014, a woman filed a complaint in an Allahabad court alleging that in 2010, the accused befriended her during coaching classes, repeatedly engaged in sexual relations under the false pretext of marriage, blackmailed her with objectionable videos, and in 2011, forced her to undergo an abortion when she became pregnant. She further alleged that when she raised the issue of marriage, the accused and his family hurled caste-based slurs at her.

Based on the complaint, the accused was charged under multiple IPC sections, including 376 (rape), 377 (unnatural offences), 323 (assault), 504 (insult), 552 (house trespass), 120 (criminal conspiracy), along with provisions of the SC/ST Act, 1989. After investigation, the Magistrate summoned the accused.

In 2019, the accused petitioned the High Court to quash the case, but the plea was dismissed. The matter then reached the Supreme Court, where the accused argued that the complaint was vague, fabricated, and motivated by malice.

Upon examining the records, the Supreme Court found glaring gaps: the complaint did not mention specific dates or locations of the alleged crimes, lacked independent corroborating evidence, and most significantly, the complainant did not even accept the notice issued by the Supreme Court. The court considered this a clear indication of her lack of seriousness.

The bench also criticized the inclusion of the accused’s parents in the case, calling it unjustified harassment. It concluded that allowing such proceedings to continue would be a misuse of justice and therefore quashed the entire criminal case.

This verdict is being seen as a strong message against false cases.

articles.title: PIL Challenges Mandatory Rollout of 20% Ethanol-Blended Petrol in India
articles.author: The Times Patriot
articles.excerpt: On August 23, Advocate Akshay Malhotra filed a Public Interest Litigation (PIL) in the Supreme Court challenging the mandatory implementation of 20% ethanol-blended petrol (E20).

body.html:
On August 23, Advocate Akshay Malhotra filed a Public Interest Litigation (PIL) in the Supreme Court challenging the mandatory implementation of 20% ethanol-blended petrol (E20).

The petitioner argued that such a policy was being imposed without adequate consumer awareness, without proper labeling, and without offering alternative options. According to him, this violated fundamental rights under Article 19(1)(a) of the Constitution, which guarantees freedom of speech and expression. He stated that the right to information and the right to make informed choices are essential parts of this fundamental right.

Further, Article 21, which guarantees the right to life and personal liberty, also includes the right to livelihood and economic well-being. Forcing consumers to use a particular fuel—especially when it could damage their vehicles and add unexpected expenses—undermines these rights. The petitioner also cited violations of the Consumer Protection Act, 2019, which requires consumers to be properly informed about the quality, quantity, potency, purity, standards, and price of goods they purchase.

The Supreme Court heard the case on September 1. Attorney General R. Venkataramani, representing the government, defended the policy, stating that the decision was taken after due consideration. He also suggested that vested interests and lobby groups might be influencing the petition.

From the petitioner’s side, Senior Advocate Sadan Farasat countered, questioning why citizens were being denied the choice of fuel and whether even basic consumer rights were being eroded.

The debate extended into the technical and environmental aspects of ethanol blending. Petrol, derived from crude oil through fractional distillation, is a fossil fuel whose extraction and combustion cause significant environmental damage, including CO₂ emissions and oil spills. The government argued that reducing dependence on fossil fuels was critical for energy security and environmental sustainability.

Ethanol, produced primarily from sugarcane molasses, maize, and surplus food grains through fermentation, was positioned as a cleaner alternative. The government projected that farmers would benefit financially from increased ethanol demand. However, critics pointed out the risks: sugarcane and maize are water-intensive crops, and large-scale ethanol production could worsen groundwater depletion, particularly in already water-stressed regions like Punjab.

The policy, initially planned for 2030, was advanced by five years, with E20 being implemented nationwide by 2025. Opposition leaders alleged conflicts of interest, pointing to companies linked to political figures that had seen sharp growth in revenue and stock prices after the ethanol policy was introduced.

Automobile compatibility is another major concern. While vehicles manufactured after 2023 are generally designed to handle E20, most of India’s existing fleet—about 89% of registered vehicles as of 2023—was made before this standard and may not run efficiently on E20. Ethanol is corrosive, can damage fuel systems, and has lower energy content than petrol, resulting in reduced mileage and higher fuel costs for consumers.

Critics also highlighted the irony of mandating ethanol-blended fuel in a country ranked poorly on the Global Hunger Index, where food security remains a pressing issue, yet food grains are being diverted toward fuel production.

The petitioner concluded that, as citizens, people should at least have the right to choose which fuel they want to use—especially one more compatible with their vehicles—rather than being compelled to accept a single option.

articles.title: Badaun Woman Elopes With Lover After 32 Years of Marriage, Husband Demands Land and Daughter Back
articles.author: The Times Patriot
articles.excerpt: Badaun, Uttar Pradesh | A shocking case has emerged from Badaun district, where a 52-year-old woman, mother of nine children, left her husband of 32 years and eloped with her lover. The case falls under the jurisdiction of Usaihat police station.

body.html:
Badaun, Uttar Pradesh | A shocking case has emerged from Badaun district, where a 52-year-old woman, mother of nine children, left her husband of 32 years and eloped with her lover. The case falls under the jurisdiction of Usaihat police station.

The woman, identified as Neelam, is married to Ompal, a resident of Kheda Jalalpur village. Ompal works in Delhi, while Neelam lived with their children in the village. Out of their nine children, three are married, while the youngest is only 10 years old.

Earlier Incident of Elopement:
According to police records, on June 2, 2025, Neelam told her children she was going to drown herself in the river. Alarmed, her youngest daughter informed Ompal, who rushed from Delhi. However, investigations revealed that Neelam had instead fled with her lover, Pappu (35), a resident of Bahediya village in Kasganj district.

Police later traced her and handed her back to her husband. Neelam assured Ompal that she would not repeat the act, and the matter was resolved.

Eloped Again With 10-Year-Old Daughter:
Barely a month later, on July 2, 2025, Neelam once again left home with Pappu—this time taking her 10-year-old daughter, Anjali, along.

Ompal lodged a complaint with the police on August 12, following which an FIR was registered on August 13 against Pappu and his brother Virendra.

Court Proceedings:
On September 10, Neelam appeared at the police station and was produced before the court. When asked whom she wished to live with, she expressed her decision to stay with her lover Pappu. The court accordingly allowed her to go with him.

Family and Property Dispute:
Ompal, devastated by the turn of events, has accused his wife of not only leaving the family but also taking jewellery, cash, and their youngest daughter. He also claimed that Neelam has possession of 3.5 bighas of agricultural land, registered in her name, which he had purchased over the years through his earnings.

“The land is worth around ₹15–18 lakh today. I worked hard to buy it, but now both my wife and property are gone. I only want my daughter and my land back,” Ompal told the police.

Family Background:
The couple has nine children—Kaushal (30), Preeti alias Pinky (25), Gaurav (22), Shivani (19), Nikhil (17), Shyamsundar (16), Akhilesh (12), and Anjali (10). Their son Neeraj (28) died by suicide last year.

The case has caused a stir in the region, with villagers expressing shock over Neelam’s decision to abandon her family at this stage of life.
